The main method is trained whereas many baselines are training-free and evaluated at different budgets; the trainable baselines are author reimplementations without enough evidence of matched data, optimization effort, or compute. The claimed architecture-agnostic applicability is also not convincingly demonstrated.

Central reproducibility details are absent: the binary correctness evaluator is undefined, and training steps or epochs, batch size, generation settings, parameter-update scheme, KL estimation, timing protocol, and random seeds are not reported. No code or model-release commitment is given, and possible overlap between Video-R1 training data and evaluation benchmarks is not analyzed.

There are material reporting contradictions. Table 3 reports Full at 70.2 and Sparsity Forcing at 70.0, while the surrounding text gives 70.0 and 70.3 and claims the proposed method is superior. Average-score normalization and the two VideoMME values are unexplained, and no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are provided despite many very small score differences.

The systems claims are under-supported: the figure describes prefill latency while the abstract claims decoding speedup; measurements up to 200k tokens are not reconciled with the approximately 20k-token evaluation setup; and hardware, precision, batch size, generated length, kernel details, warm-up, repetitions, and variability are omitted. Token-retention ratio is also not generally equivalent to FLOPs or wall-clock cost.

The core contribution is fairly incremental—applying GRPO to rollouts generated under different externally chosen sparsity thresholds—and the paper neither positions it adequately against broader learned dynamic-computation work nor supplies the ablations needed to establish that this particular RL formulation is necessary.

Includes useful budget curves, latency and memory measurements, comparisons to training-free and trainable baselines, and analyses of pruning mechanisms, context length, and hallucination robustness.

Consequently, generic post-training or distillation effects may explain part of the advantage over mostly training-free baselines.

The mathematical specification has several problems: zeroing Q/K before softmax in Eq. 2 does not implement token removal; Eq. 5 overloads p as both a retention threshold and an integer index; the GRPO distribution omits conditioning on the sampled budget; and Eq. 10 is undefined when a group has no correct answer because all rewards and their standard deviation are zero.

Baseline evidence is incomplete: learned baselines are tested on only four benchmarks, most headline tables compare methods at substantially different token ratios, and there is no full-suite comparison against a straightforward sparse SFT/distillation baseline at a matched budget and training cost.

The systems claims are underspecified. The paper calls the 3.3× result a decoding speedup, while Figure 4 labels it as prefill latency; hardware, batch size, output length, warm-up, kernel implementation, and measurement variance are not given. Sequential multi-budget training overhead is also unquantified.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem with a simple post-training idea: multi-budget GRPO jointly rewards answer correctness and token reduction without training a new architecture from scratch.
The evaluation is broad, covering four model checkpoints from two families and thirteen image/video benchmarks. Reported retention ratios of roughly 23–30% preserve performance surprisingly well.
Includes useful budget-accuracy curves, context-length analysis, HallusionBench evaluation, and measured prefill-latency/KV-memory improvements rather than reporting token counts alone.
Compares against several training-free and post-training baselines and studies pruning mechanism, threshold range, and rollout group size.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established. There is no matched correctness-only GRPO, dense-attention GRPO, efficiency-reward/group-indicator ablation, or SFT baseline using the same data and compute. Consequently, additional Video-R1/LLaVA-Video training could be compensating for pruning rather than the proposed grouped efficiency reward being essential.

The mathematical specification contains serious inconsistencies. Equation 2 zeroes Q/K entries before softmax rather than excluding masked tokens and leaves V unmasked; the stated budget counts selected queries plus keys and would give a full-attention ratio of 2 rather than 1; and the token ranking in Equations 5–7 is not consistently defined.

When no rollout is correct, the proposed safeguard makes every reward zero, so Equation 10 divides by a zero standard deviation; no epsilon or group-skipping rule is specified. The policy objective also omits conditioning on the sampled threshold, while the method samples the threshold externally rather than treating pruning decisions as policy actions.

The method description says thresholds are sampled uniformly over [0,1], whereas experiments use a narrow discretized range [0.94,0.975]. Important implementation details—including training steps, batch size, decoding settings, correctness verifier, trainable parameters, and baseline tuning—are absent, substantially limiting reproducibility.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete: runtime is reported only for one model, without hardware, batch size, kernel, warm-up, or output-length details. The 3.3x result is labeled prefill latency in Figure 4, yet the abstract and conclusion claim decoding speedup. Token-retention ratios are also not directly comparable FLOP measures across pruning methods.

No repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are provided despite many differences being below one point. Potential overlap between post-training data and evaluation sets is not analyzed, and Table 3 contains contradictory averages between the table and surrounding text.

The novelty is moderate—a GRPO wrapper around an existing ZipVL mechanism—and the claim of applicability to arbitrary sparse-attention mechanisms is supported only by simple top-k/threshold variants. Overall, the promising breadth does not overcome the soundness, attribution, and reproducibility gaps for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing multimodal-LLM inference cost while preserving answer quality.

The proposed combination of multi-budget rollouts, correctness rewards, and efficiency rewards is simple and potentially useful. The group-level gate that disables the efficiency reward when no rollout is correct is intuitively motivated.

The empirical scope is broad: four model configurations, thirteen image/video benchmarks, several sparse-attention baselines, budget sweeps, a hallucination benchmark, and latency/memory measurements.
If independently reproducible, retaining roughly 23–30% of tokens while approaching dense-model accuracy would be a practically significant result.
The paper is generally readable, and the budget-performance curves and layer-wise sparsity analysis help communicate the intended behavior.
weaknesses: The central optimization claim is not technically established. The retention threshold and discrete mask are externally chosen rather than modeled as policy actions, while the GRPO likelihood concerns only generated text and even omits conditioning on the threshold. Because token ratio also depends directly and non-differentiably on the model parameters, the stated objective does not explain valid credit assignment to token-selection decisions. Calling this end-to-end optimization of sparsity is therefore insufficiently justified.

The sparse-attention formalization is incorrect. In Eq. 2, multiplying keys by zero before softmax does not remove them: zero logits still receive positive softmax mass, and masked queries produce uniform attention; values are not masked either. Eq. 3 uses an additive query/key token count although attention cost depends on their interaction, and its global retained-mass constraint does not imply the stated per-output approximation guarantee. Eq. 5 also overloads the retention threshold as an integer index.

Essential controls are absent. There is no accuracy-only GRPO, efficiency-reward ablation, group-gating ablation, fixed-budget versus multi-budget training comparison, same-data SFT control, or dense post-trained control. Consequently, the results do not isolate whether the gains arise from the proposed reward, ordinary post-training on 260k examples, or another component.

Baseline fairness is unclear. The strongest headline comparisons pit a trained method against training-free methods, while training recipes and compute for MOBA and the sharpness-loss baseline are largely unspecified. Several comparisons also use unmatched token ratios, preventing a clean Pareto-frontier comparison.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The method states both p sampled uniformly from [0,1] and a discrete training range [0.94,0.975]; group size 12 is reported despite that stepped range containing only eight values. Training duration, effective batch size, GRPO clipping value, generation settings, correctness evaluator, trainable-parameter choice, and sparse-kernel implementation are omitted. Moreover, reward normalization is undefined when all rewards are equal—especially when no rollout is correct and every reward is zero.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates or multiple seeds even though many reported accuracy differences are only 0.1–0.4 points. There is also no analysis of overlap or contamination between the large public post-training corpora and the thirteen evaluation benchmarks.

Efficiency claims are underdocumented and internally inconsistent. Figure 4 measures prefill latency, whereas the abstract and conclusion claim a 3.3× decoding speedup. The 200k-token timing setup, hardware, precision, batch size, warm-up protocol, output length, and baseline kernel configuration are not reported; actual task evaluation uses only about 16k–20k tokens.

Several reporting inconsistencies further reduce confidence: the Table 3 narrative gives different averages from the table, average-score normalization is unexplained, and the HallusionBench experiment does not report its supposedly strict token budget or exact numerical results.

The novelty discussion is too narrow. The work is mainly a straightforward application of grouped policy optimization to a budgeted-computation objective, but it is not adequately positioned against broader learned token-pruning, adaptive-computation, and budget-aware inference literature. Overall, the promising empirical direction is outweighed by unresolved soundness, attribution, and reproducibility issues.
